    The parable

    Learning is training

    Walk into any gym on January 2nd. You'll see beginners loading every plate onto the bar, determined to get fit by Friday. Walk in on March 2nd — they're gone.

    A

    The Beginner's Mistake

    Day one: six courses, three textbooks, a 12-hour marathon. By day three — burnout, frustration, and nothing retained.

    • 01Lift the heaviest weight on day one
    • 02Train every muscle group daily
    • 03Push through pain and exhaustion
    • 04Expect visible results in a week
    B

    The Professional Athlete

    Elite athletes never train at 100% every day. They use periodisation — scientifically timed cycles of intensity and recovery.

    • 01Progressive overload — increase weight gradually
    • 02Periodised training — planned rest and recovery
    • 03Muscle memory — spaced sessions build lasting strength
    • 04Deload weeks — strategic lighter periods for growth

    Metability is your training programme for the brain

    Metability applies the same logic to learning: the right load, the right day, built-in recovery. No cramming. No forgetting. Steady compounding — peaking when it matters.

    Project AMBER — EU curriculum graph

    The national curriculum, as a living graph

    Curricula are published as documents. Learning happens as a graph — every topic depends on earlier ones. AMBER encodes official EU and Lithuanian frameworks into one prerequisite graph the retention engine can act on: what does this learner know, what is decaying, what must be reviewed next.

    Prerequisites made explicit

    Every micro-topic carries hand-reasoned prerequisite edges — so the retention engine can schedule the review that unblocks the next step, per student.

    Open by design

    The science

    140 years in the making

    From Ebbinghaus's 1885 experiments to today's scheduling engines — the science behind your study plan.

    1885

    The Pioneer

    In 1885, German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus locked himself in a room with lists of made-up syllables — DAX, BUP, ZOL — and tested his own memory over days, weeks, and months. He became both scientist and guinea pig. What he found changed everything we know about learning.

    1885+

    The Forgetting Curve

    Ebbinghaus proved that without review, you forget more than half of what you learn within an hour. After a month, barely 20% remains. But he also discovered something hopeful: a single well-timed review could dramatically slow the decay. He called it the 'spacing effect.'

    2014

    The Populariser

    For over a century, these findings stayed locked in academic journals. Then in 2014, New York Times science reporter Benedict Carey published 'How We Learn' — translating decades of cognitive research into practical strategies anyone could use. Millions discovered that everything they believed about studying was wrong.

    Today

    The Modern Engine

    Today, peer-reviewed algorithms build on 140 years of memory science — from Ebbinghaus to Pimsleur, Leitner, and modern computational models. They calculate the precise moment to review — not too early (wasted effort), not too late (forgotten). That engine powers Metability.

    The forgetting curve is real
